Two of your friends are much more likely to know each other than two people chosen at random. This
tendency, called *triadic closure*, fills social networks with triangles, and similar small
patterns recur throughout networks of every kind: feed-forward loops in gene regulation, cycles in
food webs, and chains of command in organizations. This page covers the measures of local
structure: triangles and clustering coefficients, counts of small subgraphs called *motifs*, the
triad census of directed graphs, and cycles.

## Triangles

A triangle is three nodes that are all linked to one another, the smallest possible group of mutual
friends. [`count_triangles()`](../reference/Graph.count_triangles.qmd) returns the number of
triangles each node belongs to, and [`list_triangles()`](../reference/Graph.list_triangles.qmd)
lists them all as triples of node IDs:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
triangles = karate.count_triangles()
len(karate.list_triangles()), triangles[1]
```

The karate club contains 45 triangles, and the instructor (ID 1) belongs to 18 of them. Since every
triangle has three corners, the per-node counts add up to three times the total.

## Clustering coefficients

A node's *local clustering coefficient* is the fraction of pairs of its neighbors that are
themselves linked, or equivalently the number of triangles it belongs to divided by the number it
could belong to. A coefficient of 1 means that a node's neighbors form a clique, and 0 means that
none of them know each other.

Two methods compute it. [`clustering_coefficient()`](../reference/Graph.clustering_coefficient.qmd)
gives nodes with fewer than two neighbors, which can't belong to any triangle, a coefficient of 0.
[`local_clustering_coefficient()`](../reference/Graph.local_clustering_coefficient.qmd) leaves
them undefined, as `None`, which keeps them out of averages:

```{python}
karate.clustering_coefficient().local_clustering_coefficient()
(
    karate.get_node_df()
    .select("id", "label", "degree", "clustering_coefficient", "local_clustering_coefficient")
    .filter(pl.col("id").is_in([1, 12, 34]))
)
```

The two leaders have low clustering. The instructor's 16 friends could form 120 pairs, but only 18
of those pairs are friends themselves; the leaders' circles span groups that don't otherwise mix.
Member `"11"` (ID 12), with a single friend, has a coefficient of 0 or `None`, depending on the
method.

### Two global measures

There are two common ways to summarize clustering for a whole graph, and they can differ a great
deal. [`get_avg_clustering_coefficient()`](../reference/Graph.get_avg_clustering_coefficient.qmd)
averages the local coefficients over the nodes, while
[`get_transitivity()`](../reference/Graph.get_transitivity.qmd) is the fraction of all connected
triples of nodes (paths of two edges) that are closed into triangles. Transitivity weights each
node by the number of pairs of neighbors it has, so it is dominated by the hubs:

```{python}
round(karate.get_avg_clustering_coefficient(), 3), round(karate.get_transitivity(), 3)
```

In the karate club, the average is more than double the transitivity, because the many low-degree
members have tightly knit neighborhoods while the two hubs do not. Report which measure you use,
since both go by the name "clustering coefficient".

The question that matters is usually whether clustering is *higher than expected*. A degree-
preserving randomization, from [`random_reference()`](../reference/Graph.random_reference.qmd),
keeps every node's degree but rewires the edges at random, and so shows how much clustering the
degrees alone would produce. Comparing several networks with their randomized versions
(simplified first, since some of the bundled networks contain duplicate edges; see
[Datasets](06-datasets.qmd#networks-from-data-repositories)):

```{python}
networks = {
    "karate club": karate,
    "dolphins": ec.dolphins(),
    "jazz musicians": ec.jazz().simplify(),
    "power grid": ec.power_grid(),
    "co-authorship (ca_grqc)": ec.ca_grqc().simplify(),
    "Internet": ec.internet().simplify(),
}
pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "network": name,
            "average": round(graph.get_avg_clustering_coefficient(), 3),
            "transitivity": round(graph.get_transitivity(), 3),
            "randomized": round(graph.random_reference(seed=1).get_transitivity(), 3),
        }
        for name, graph in networks.items()
    ]
)
```

The co-authorship network is the most strongly clustered: a paper with several authors creates a
clique among them, and its transitivity of 0.63 is fifty times the randomized value. The power grid
also has far more triangles than its degrees imply, a consequence of its geography. The Internet is
the exception, and an instructive one. Its average clustering is high, but its transitivity is no
higher than chance: the many small networks that connect to the same few providers form triangles
with them, while the providers themselves, with thousands of neighbors, have almost none.

### Clustering and degree

In many networks, clustering falls as degree rises: low-degree nodes sit in small, tight groups,
and high-degree nodes bridge between them. Grouping the node table by degree shows the pattern in
the co-authorship network:

```{python}
coauthors = ec.ca_grqc().simplify().clustering_coefficient()
(
    coauthors.get_node_df()
    .filter(pl.col("degree").is_between(2, 10))
    .group_by("degree")
    .agg(pl.col("clustering_coefficient").mean().round(3), authors=pl.len())
    .sort("degree")
)
```

Authors with two collaborators usually wrote one paper with both of them, so their clustering is
close to 1. Authors with ten collaborators have worked with several separate groups, and only a
third of their pairs of collaborators have written together. This decline is often taken as a sign
of hierarchical organization, with small groups nested inside larger ones.

### Other coefficients

Several variants of clustering suit other questions:

| Method | Measures |
|---|---|
| [`square_clustering()`](../reference/Graph.square_clustering.qmd) | the fraction of possible squares (four-cycles) through a node; useful in bipartite-like networks, which have no triangles |
| [`get_edge_clustering_coefficient()`](../reference/Graph.get_edge_clustering_coefficient.qmd) | the triangles (or squares, with `k=4`) through an edge, relative to the fewest its endpoints allow |
| [`generalized_degree()`](../reference/Graph.generalized_degree.qmd) | a node's edges, counted by how many triangles each belongs to |
| [`latapy_clustering()`](../reference/Graph.latapy_clustering.qmd), [`robins_alexander_clustering()`](../reference/Graph.robins_alexander_clustering.qmd) | clustering for bipartite graphs |

For directed graphs, `local_clustering_coefficient()` counts triangles among a node's successors.
[Structural properties](11-structure.qmd#cliques) covers cliques, the extreme form of clustering.

## Motifs

Triangles are one of two shapes that three connected nodes can form; the other is a path, in which
one pair is not linked. More generally, a *motif* is a small pattern of connections, and counting
the motifs of a network gives a fingerprint of its local wiring.
[`motif_census()`](../reference/Graph.motif_census.qmd) counts every connected group of three
nodes (or four, with `size=4`) by its shape. The groups are *induced*, which means each is
classified by all the edges among its nodes, so a triangle isn't also counted as a path:

```{python}
karate.motif_census()
```

On its own, a count says little. A network with high-degree nodes contains many triangles simply
because hubs have many pairs of neighbors. The usual test compares the observed counts with those
of many degree-preserving randomizations of the same network, and expresses the difference as a
*z-score*: the number of standard deviations by which the observed count exceeds the randomized
average. A short function does this with `random_reference()`:

```{python}
import statistics


def motif_z_scores(graph, size=3, n_random=30):
    observed = graph.motif_census(size=size)
    randomized = [
        graph.random_reference(niter=10, seed=seed).motif_census(size=size)
        for seed in range(n_random)
    ]
    scores = {}
    for shape, count in observed.items():
        counts = [census.get(shape, 0) for census in randomized]
        scores[shape] = round((count - statistics.mean(counts)) / statistics.stdev(counts), 1)
    return scores


dolphins = ec.dolphins()
dolphins.motif_census(), motif_z_scores(dolphins)
```

The `niter=10` argument rewires each edge about ten times, enough to erase the original structure,
and `census.get(shape, 0)` covers randomizations in which a shape doesn't occur at all. The
dolphins form 95 triangles, where their degrees alone would give about 33, a difference of more
than fourteen standard deviations. Associations among dolphins are strongly transitive. (The path
score is the mirror image of the triangle score, because with every degree fixed, each extra
triangle uses up three paths.) The same
test on the karate club gives a z-score of only about 1.4, since its 45 triangles are not many more
than the 39 or so its two hubs produce by themselves; this agrees with the modest gap between the
karate club's transitivity and the randomized value in the table above.

Motifs with large positive z-scores are a network's characteristic building blocks, and those with
large negative ones are patterns it avoids. Four-node motifs reveal more, at a higher cost:

```{python}
motif_z_scores(dolphins, size=4)
```

The fully connected `"clique_4"`, and the `"near_clique_4"` that lacks a single edge, are far more
common among the dolphins than chance would allow. The other four-node shapes have generated names,
of the form `motif_4e<edges>_k<key>`, that give their number of edges and an internal code. Of the
two with three edges, `motif_4e3_k591` is the star, one node linked to the other three, and
`motif_4e3_k669` is the path; both are rarer than chance, because the dolphins' open triples tend to
close. Of the two with four edges, `motif_4e4_k735` is a triangle with one extra node attached and
`motif_4e4_k1782` is the square, a four-cycle without diagonals.

[`motif_significance()`](../reference/Graph.motif_significance.qmd) packages the same kind of test,
with `n_random=` randomizations, and reports a z-score and a p-value for each shape. Because every
group of nodes must be examined, a census costs roughly `n³` operations for `size=3` and `n⁴` for
`size=4`. Both are best kept to graphs of a few hundred nodes, and a significance test multiplies
the cost by the number of randomizations.

## Triads in directed graphs

In a directed graph, each pair of nodes is linked in both directions, in one, or not at all, so
three nodes can form 16 different *triads*. They are named with the standard MAN codes, three
digits that count the **M**utual, **A**symmetric, and **N**ull pairs, and a letter to tell apart
types with the same counts (**D**own, **U**p, **C**yclic, and **T**ransitive).
[`triad_type()`](../reference/Graph.triad_type.qmd) classifies a single triad:

```{python}
small = ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")], directed=True
)
small.triad_type(["A", "B", "C"]), small.triad_type(["A", "C", "D"]), small.triad_type(["B", "C", "D"])
```

`A`, `B`, and `C` form a *transitive* triad (`030T`), in which `A` reaches `C` both directly and
by way of `B`. `A`, `C`, and `D` form a *cycle* (`030C`), and `B`, `C`, and `D` a chain (`021C`)
with no edge between its ends.

[`triadic_census()`](../reference/Graph.triadic_census.qmd) counts every triad in the graph. It
only visits connected triads, so it runs quickly even on large sparse networks. For the Wikipedia
election network, the comparison between transitive and cyclic triads is telling:

```{python}
census = ec.wiki_vote().triadic_census()
census["030T"], census["030C"]
```

In a random directed graph, transitive triads would outnumber cyclic ones by about three to one,
since there are three times as many ways to arrange three one-way edges transitively. In the
election network the ratio is nearly seventy to one. Votes flow from less established users to
more established ones, and rarely around a loop, which is the signature of a status hierarchy.
[`triads_by_type()`](../reference/Graph.triads_by_type.qmd) lists the triads of each type, and
[`all_triads()`](../reference/Graph.all_triads.qmd) lists every triad of a graph.

## Cycles

A cycle is a path that returns to its start without repeating a node. Triangles are the shortest
possible cycles in a simple graph, and [`get_girth()`](../reference/Graph.get_girth.qmd) returns
the length of a graph's shortest cycle, or `None` if it has none:

```{python}
karate.get_girth()
```

Listing every cycle is rarely practical, since their number grows exponentially with the size of
a graph. A *cycle basis* is a small set of cycles from which every other cycle can be built, by
combining cycles and cancelling out the edges they share. Every basis of a connected graph has
`m - n + 1` cycles, where `m` is the number of edges and `n` the number of nodes, so this number,
the *cyclomatic number*, measures how far a graph is from being a tree:

```{python}
basis = karate.cycle_basis()
len(basis), karate.count_edges() - karate.count_nodes() + 1
```

[`cycle_basis()`](../reference/Graph.cycle_basis.qmd) finds a basis quickly, and
[`minimum_cycle_basis()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_cycle_basis.qmd) finds one whose cycles are
as short as possible, which is more useful for analysis, such as finding the rings of a molecule.
The other cycle methods are these:

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| [`simple_cycles()`](../reference/Graph.simple_cycles.qmd) | every cycle, optionally only those up to `length_bound=` nodes |
| [`get_cycles()`](../reference/Graph.get_cycles.qmd) | every cycle of at least `min_length=` nodes (Johnson's algorithm) |
| [`directed_cycle_basis()`](../reference/Graph.directed_cycle_basis.qmd) | a cycle basis that respects edge direction |
| [`minimum_feedback_edge_set()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_feedback_edge_set.qmd) | the lightest set of edges whose removal leaves no cycles |
| [`has_cycles()`](../reference/Graph.has_cycles.qmd), [`is_dag()`](../reference/Graph.is_dag.qmd) | whether a graph has any cycles, and whether a directed graph has none |

In a directed graph, cycles must follow edge direction. The small graph above has two:

```{python}
[[small.get_label_from_id(node) for node in cycle] for cycle in small.simple_cycles()]
```

`C` leads to `D`, `D` to `A`, and `A` back to `C`, either directly or by way of `B`. Bounding the
length keeps the enumeration manageable on larger graphs: in the karate club,
`simple_cycles(length_bound=4)` finds the 199 cycles of three or four members. Directed graphs
without any cycles are the subject of [Directed acyclic graphs](17-dags.qmd).
